extracted.intended_audience: applicants to NIH grant programs, institutional sponsored programs staff, and NIH peer reviewers/administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the Scientific Review Group (SRG) first-level peer review process for NIH grant applications, covering reviewer roles, review criteria, scoring, summary statements, conflicts of interest, and appeals. Intended to inform how applications are evaluated and how applicants receive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the overall impact that the proposed project will likely have on the biomedical research field(s) involved; impact scores reflect the reviewers’ overall assessment of the likelihood for the project to exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field(s) involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers give a preliminary Overall Impact score before the meeting and final eligible panelists give final impact scores for discussed applications. A final Overall Impact score is the mean of final impact scores multiplied by 10, yielding scores from 10 (high impact) through 90 (low impact). Reviewers use their judgment to determine how individual criteria weigh into the Overall Impact score (unless funding opportunity specifies otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scored Review Criteria (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each grant application is evaluated according to established review criteria that must be stated clearly in a notice of funding opportunity; for most application types these are defined in NIH Peer Review regulations but may be re-defined or supplemented by the funding opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assign individual criterion scores for all scored review criteria. Criterion scores typically use a numerical scale of 1 to 9 (1 = exceptional; 9 = poor) in whole numbers. The individual scores from assigned reviewers for these criteria are provided to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Review Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria that do not receive individual criterion scores but do contribute to the Overall Impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some additional review criteria need to be considered acceptable before the NIH can award a grant (for example, protections for human subjects, vertebrate animals, and biohazards). Reviewers must consider these areas and report concerns that affect awardability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Review Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters that do not receive individual criterion scores and do not contribute to the Overall Impact score but provide expert input on programmatic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to solicit input that does not directly reflect scientific and technical merit. Examples include whether the budget is sufficiently justified, or whether the project could be completed for a smaller budget or fewer years than requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections for Human Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the adequacy of protections for human subjects involved in the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is treated as an additional review criterion that may need to be acceptable before the NIH can award a grant. Reviewers make recommendations concerning protections for human subjects and consult detailed guidance for reviewers on Human Subjects Protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Women, Minorities, and Children
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of plans for inclusion of women, minorities, and children in clinical research as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers make recommendations concerning inclusion and consult NIH inclusion guidance. Inclusion considerations are among the additional review criteria that can affect awardability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebrate Animal Protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the appropriateness of proposed use and welfare protections for vertebrate animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered an additional review criterion that must often be acceptable before award; reviewers consult NIH guidance on vertebrate animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Embryonic Stem Cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of proposed use of human embryonic stem cells where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addressed as an additional review criterion with specific NIH guidance to be followed; acceptability may be required for award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biohazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of biohazard risks and adequacy of proposed protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered an additional review criterion; must often be acceptable before award. Reviewers make recommendations regarding biohazard safety and containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget Appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of whether the requested budget is appropriate and justified for the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may be asked whether the budget is sufficiently justified, or whether the project could be completed for a smaller budget or fewer years. Budget questions are typically treated as additional review considerations and may be included in the summary statement as budget recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and Resources (sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the investigators and institutional resources are sufficient to carry out the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many research grants this factor may be evaluated qualitatively as either sufficient or not. Reviewers assign criterion scores and may comment on adequacy of expertise, team composition, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring Process and Scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics of scoring: individual criterion scores and overall impact use a numerical scale; process for preliminary and final scoring and percentile calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH uses a 9-point rating scale (1 = exceptional; 9 = poor) in whole numbers. Assigned reviewers give separate scores for each review criterion and a preliminary Overall Impact score before the meeting; preliminary scores are often used to triage which applications are fully discussed. For discussed applications, eligible panelists give final Overall Impact scores; the mean final impact score is multiplied by 10 to produce a 10–90 scale. Percentiles (when provided) rank an application's impact score relative to other applications reviewed by that SRG across recent rounds. Not Discussed (ND) applications (typically bottom half) are not discussed and do not receive a numerical final Overall Impact score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Selection Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for recruiting and vetting reviewers who serve on Scientific Review Groups (SRGs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SROs recruit qualified reviewers based on scientific and technical qualifications and other considerations, including authority in their scientific field, dedication to high quality, fair, and objective reviews, ability to work collegially in a group setting, and balanced expertise appropriate for the applications under review. Reviewers are fully vetted for appropriate expertise, potential conflicts of interest, and other requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest Management
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures to identify and manage conflicts of interest among reviewers and meeting participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must declare conflicts of interest with specific applications following NIH guidance. Any reviewer with a conflict is asked to leave the room before that application is reviewed. The SRO actively manages conflicts of interest and ensures compliance with review policy. Applicants may not contact reviewers to influence the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of Review Meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Review meetings and peer review information are confidential and should not be disclosed outside the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are reminded that NIH review meetings are confidential and not to divulge any information outside the meeting; integrity and confidentiality policies apply and violations have consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigned Reviewers and Pre-Meeting Responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO assigns at least three reviewers to each application; assigned reviewers prepare critiques and preliminary scores before the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigned reviewers receive access to applications approximately six weeks prior to the meeting, read each assigned application thoroughly, write a critique summarizing strengths and weaknesses, and assign a preliminary Overall Impact score. The SRO provides instructions on critique preparation and assignment of individual criterion scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Scientific Review Officer (SRO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO is responsible for ensuring objective, fair initial peer review and compliance with laws, regulations, and policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SRO assigns reviewers, manages the peer review meeting to ensure fair and effective review (including conflicts of interest and regulatory aspects), and prepares a resume of discussion to reflect score-driving elements. Federal officials may attend with SRO approval when they have a need-to-know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Chair and Reviewers During Meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Chair moderates discussion and serves as a reviewer; reviewers present assigned critiques and participate in discussion and scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the meeting the primary reviewer presents the application and leads discussion; the other two assigned reviewers can provide additional comments. All panelists not in conflict (not just assigned reviewers) discuss and score the application. The chair facilitates discussion and also participates as a reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary Statement Contents and Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Information provided to applicants after review, including impact scores, critiques, and administrative comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the meeting, all reviewed applications receive an impact score and a summary statement prepared by the SRO. NIH typically releases scores in eRA Commons within 3 business days and uploads the summary statement within about 30 days. The summary statement includes Impact Score and Percentile (if applicable), brief summary of the SRG discussion, criterion scores from the assigned reviewers, bulleted critiques (strengths and weaknesses) from the assigned reviewer, budget recommendations, and any administrative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals Grounds and Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria under which investigators or applicant organizations may seek reconsideration of the initial review results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH's peer review appeal system permits appeals if applicants believe the review process was flawed due to bias of a reviewer, conflict of interest, absence of appropriate expertise, or factual errors by one or more reviewers that could have substantially altered the review outcome. The policy does not apply to appeals of funding decisions or certain other determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Discussed (ND) Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule for applications that will not be discussed at the SRG meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications unanimously judged by the SRG to be less competitive (typically rank in the bottom half) are not discussed at the meeting and do not receive a numerical final Overall Impact score. Preliminary scores are often used to triage which applications will be discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application Presentation for Scannability
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for applicants to prepare applications so reviewers who are scanning can understand and find information quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tip to applicants: while assigned reviewers read your application carefully, many reviewers will be scanning it as they listen to the discussion — prepare your application so it is easy for someone scanning to understand what you are proposing and find the information they are looking for.
